title: 100% EASIEST WAY TO PLAY "Country Roads" on Guitar | Lesson for Beginners
description:
Welcome to my "Country Roads" Guitar Lesson + Tutorial, by John Denver. This is one of the easiest songs on guitar, using 4 basic chords and a beginner strumming pattern. Learn how to play Country Roads on the guitar in the simplest way possible with this easy strumming version for acoustic guitar!

"Country Roads" CHORDS: G, C, D, Em

"Country Roads" STRUMMING PATTERN: D D -uDu

► "Country Roads" FULL SONG PLAY-THROUGH (play along with me, from start-to-finish) available on my Patreon page:
https://www.patreon.com/posts/67741779/

► Grab your copy of my FREE E-BOOK!
https://goodguitarist.com/learn-rhythm-guitar/

► Need help with the basic chords and strumming? My BEGINNER GUITAR COURSE will help you build a solid foundation one step at a time:
https://goodguitarist.com/beginner-guitar-course/

► Ready to take strumming to the next level? STRUMMING MADE SIMPLE (from Beginner To Advanced) will teach you how to play + sing at the same time, make your own patterns and more:
https://goodguitarist.com/strumming-made-simple/

"Country Roads" TABLE OF CONTENTS

0:00 - INTRO
1:24 - CHORDS + SWITCHING TIPS
2:36 - SWITCHING PRACTICE
3:43 - STRUMMING PATTERN
6:00 - CHORUS PLAY-ALONG
7 :55 - THE VERSE
8:06 - VERSE PLAY-ALONG
9:01 - THE BRIDGE
10:58 - SONG FORM 
11:47 - TIPS + RESOURCES

The lesson begins with the chord shapes needed to play this song: G, D, Em, C. There are two tricks that I'd like to show you. When switching from G to D, we can leave our ring finger down, pivot off of that finger and it'll make the switch so much smoother and easier. When switching from E minor to C, we can do the same thing but pivoting off our middle finger this time. With those tips in mind, we strum through the chord shapes using downstrokes only, keeping the rhythm as simple as possible, counting along and playing through the chorus.

After becoming familiar with the chord shapes, we take a look at the strumming pattern. I've chosen a pattern that is very simple, but fits the feeling of the song perfectly. We go through it, breaking it down, counting it out, learning to feel the rhythm and then putting it all together with our chord progression. We play the chorus together, slowly, to give you a chance to feel what it's like to play along with another guitarist.

We apply the same concept to the verse and the bridge. The verse has an extra measure. We learn how to count it and adjust our strumming pattern accordingly. The bridge has an extra chord. It's an F chord that we play one time and it's very similar to C. I have an easy version of it that's totally possible for even a beginner to play (instead of that dreaded F barre chord!). After learning each part of the song, we learn how the whole thing goes together.

If you'd like to practice the entire song with me, there's a full playthrough available on my Patreon page, where I play through the entire song, start to finish. More information on that here: https://www.patreon.com/posts/67741779/

title: Alice in Chains - Nutshell guitar lesson for beginners
description:
Alice in Chains - Nutshell guitar lesson for beginners
Found this useful? Please consider supporting me!
Buy me a coffee: https://www.buymeacoffee.com/LeftHandedMatt
Support me on Patreon: http://www.patreon.com/LeftHandedGuitarist

These videos are designed for guitar beginners or those with only limited guitar knowledge. They use simple chord shapes as much as possible and do not necessarily represent the way in which the song was originally played. They are designed as practice tools to supplement your other learning methods. Information is provided on screen for both right and left-handed players!

Like most Alice In Chains songs, Nutshell was originally recorded in Eb tuning, meaning the guitars are all tuned a half-step down. I've done this lesson in standard tuning so it doesn't match up to the recording, but the chord shapes used are correct. To change into Eb tuning you just need to drop each string on your guitar down by one note (low to high: Eb-Ab-Db-Gb-Bb-Eb). Alternatively, many computers will be able to pitch shift the song by +1 in the audio control settings so it matches standard tuning.

Nutshell is a very simple song from a chord point of view, but what makes it a bit tricky is the strange rhythm and timing of the chord changes. If you're not comfortable doing complicated strum patterns yet it's best to just try and get the chord changes down first and not worry about strumming. This is very much a feel piece so get familiar with when the changes are happening.

There are some little embellishments to the Cadd9 chords as you play, these can be improvised or skipped. I included them in the chord diagrams where I played them. Enjoy!

1. Budget 
- This is just an estimate of your income and expenses and whatever money you have left 
- This is what's going to help you keep track of your money and make sure you don’t spend it all on trash like I did 
- I use the simple Budget 

Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2iqN4KT8eo&t=1s

2. Emergency Account 
- This money you put aside for the unknown, things you can't predict 
- Like illness, losing your job, or someone passing away in your family 
- The rule is you save 3-6 month worth of monthly expenses 

Why: so when things go wrong and they will, you have money set aside to live off yourself for 3-6 months 

3. Sinking Funds 
- This is money you save for the Knowns, thing you know will happen so you save up for it 
- You should know your car is going to break down, your house will need maintenance, or that you want to go on vacation or that you want to buy aunt JJ something for Christmas ( so you start saving money up for it now ) 
- This will help prevent you from going into debt 

4. Interest Rate 
- Is the percentage of the money you will be charged on the amount of money you borrowed aka principle 
- So if a lender ever tells you your interest rate 25%, they are going to charge you 25% on the money you borrowed which is a lot 

Tip: this can also be used for investment, how much interest will I earn on the money invested, and so on

5. APY vs APR

Full Article: https://www.investopedia.com/personal-finance/apr-apy-bank-hopes-cant-tell-difference/

6. Networth 
- This is very important ( its basically Assets – Liabilities = Networth ) 
- So the means what you won – what you own = networth 
- If you have a car you own that but if you have a loan you owe that 

7. Passive iNcome 
- Is money that you earned without having to actively do a lot of work for it ( usually require a lot of work upfront and then some maintenance along the way ) 
- Takes a lot of work to buy real estate, but less work to collect rents 
- Takes a lot of work to buy stocks but less work to collect dividends 

8. Compound interest 
- Is allowing your principle and your interest to be added, so that way you earn more principle 

9. Credit Score ( just means servicing Debt, and you don’t need one to buy a house ) 
- Your credit score is just a number/rating for the person you want to borrow money from to see how you manage debt 
- But you don’t need it to buy a house, they just analyze your situation manually 
- But if you want to put it the best way is to ( use the one bill method)

10. Leverage ( usually using OPM, other people money to make money) 
- The idea is to use debt most of the time 
- And that once the transaction is completed to pocket some money ( it can enhance the amount of money you can make but can also enhance your losses ) 
- I borrowed 28,800 for 3.75% for 30 years 
- I don’t recommend you do this 

11. Margin of Safety 
- This is common knowledge but not really used 
- Its have a percentage of safety in each deal you buy 
- It's how an elevator might say the limit is 1000lbs but in reality it's 1250 ( just in case)

12. Equity 
- Is the amount of ownership you have in assets that might have debt on it 
- So If I borrowed 100k for my house but I already paid 25k towards the capital 
- I have 25k in equity

title: 7 Weird Money Habits That Are Secretly Genius
description:
Most people think building wealth means cutting lattes and budgeting harder. They're wrong.
In this video, I run the actual math on 7 counterintuitive money habits — including why investing while in debt can net you $39,200 more.
🔢 The numbers will surprise you.

Two people. Same salary. Same starting point.
10 years later — one has $310,000. The other has $41,000.
The difference isn't income. It's which smart money habits they used.

The one with $310,000 did things that looked financially irresponsible:
invested while carrying debt, didn't pay off the mortgage early, drove 
a 3-year-old used car, and never actively managed a single investment.

The "responsible" one followed every rule. Saved first. Paid off debt.
Waited until everything was in order before investing.

The math tells a different story.

In this video, I break down 7 financial habits that look completely wrong 
— until you run the actual numbers. You'll see why delaying investment 
by just 2 years costs $247,000 at retirement. Why one new car purchase 
silently drains $163,000 from your future. And why the wealthiest 
Americans automate their money at nearly twice the rate of average earners.

These aren't opinions. Every number in this video comes from JP Morgan, 
Vanguard, Edmunds, DALBAR, and the Federal Reserve.

This is the math they never taught you.

title: Simpson's Rule | Calculus Lesson 41 - JK Math
description:
How To Use Simpson’s Rule To Approximate Area (Calculus Lesson 41)

➡️ Download My Free Calculus 1 Worksheets: https://www.jkmathematics.com/calculus1-worksheet-set

🖥️ Join My Membership Site: https://www.jkmathematics.com/plus

In this lesson we learn how to use Simpson’s rule to approximate the area under the curve of a function. Simpson’s rule approximates the area using second-degree polynomials rather than first-degree polynomials like the trapezoidal rule uses. We discuss how as a result of this, Simpson’s rule yields a more accurate approximation of the area under the curve than any of the previous methods we have looked at and compare the approximation to the actual area under the curve using a definite integral.

This course is designed to help students understand the concepts of calculus at a grounded level. No long, boring, and unnecessary explanations, just what you need to know at a reasonable and digestible pace, with each lesson under 20 minutes!

title: Subspaces are the Natural Subsets of Linear Algebra | Definition + First Examples
description:
A subspace is a subset that respects the two basic operations of linear algebra: vector addition and scalar multiplication. We say they are "closed under vector addition" and "closed under scalar multiplication". On a subspace, you can do linear algebra! Indeed, a subspace is an example of a vector space. We see that all of R^n, {0}, and lines through the origin are all subspaces, but that lines NOT through the origin are not subspaces.

**************************************************

map(): Applies a function to every element of an iterable.

elif: Checks another condition if the previous one is false.
else: Executes when all conditions are false.
while loop: Repeats code while a condition is true.

title: Python Tutorial #6 - Basic Input and Output in Python Programming
description:
Basic Input and Output in Python Programming for Beginners
In this video by Programming for beginners we will see Basic Input and Output in Python Programming for Beginners, in Python tutorial for beginners series.
Python programming language is very easy to learn for students and professionals.

In this tutorial, we will learn simple ways to display output to users and take input from users in Python with the help of examples.
In Python, we can simply use the print() function to print output.

The actual syntax of the print function accepts 5 parameters:
print(object= separator= end= file= flush=)

- object - value(s) to be printed
- sep (optional) - allows us to separate multiple objects inside print().
- end (optional) - allows us to add specific values like new line "\n", tab "\t"
- file (optional) - where the values are printed. It's default value is sys.stdout (screen)
- flush (optional) - boolean specifying if the output is flushed or buffered. Default: False

Python Input
While programming, we might want to take the input from the user. In Python, we can use the input() function.

num = input("Enter a number: ")

Easy trick:

- *args → unlimited values

Common mistake:

- Thinking args name is compulsory

Quick revision:

- Stores values as tuple
- Useful when number of inputs is unknown

title: Python FastAPI Tutorial: Full Course for Beginners - Build a Full-Stack Web App
description:
In this video, we'll be learning how to build a full-featured web application from the ground up using the FastAPI framework in Python. This is the complete series compiled into one long video, covering everything from creating your first route all the way through deploying a production-ready application with a custom domain. We'll build both a JSON API for programmatic access and HTML pages that users can browse in the browser, so you'll come away knowing how to use FastAPI for either purpose.

Along the way, we'll set up a database with SQLAlchemy, write Pydantic models for request and response validation, and implement complete CRUD operations. We'll add user registration and login with secure password hashing and JWT authentication, protect routes by verifying the current user, and handle file uploads with image processing and validation. We'll convert our app to async, organize our code with routers, build out frontend forms that connect to the API with JavaScript, and add pagination, password reset flows with background email tasks, and database migrations with Alembic. Toward the end, we'll move from SQLite to PostgreSQL, move our file storage from local disk to AWS S3 with Boto3, write tests with Pytest, and finally deploy the application two different ways... first to a VPS with Nginx and SSL, and then with Docker to a serverless container platform.

Whether you're new to FastAPI or have used it for small projects and want to see how a real production application comes together, this video will give you a solid foundation. Let's get started...

Timestamps:
(00:00:00) Getting Started - Web App + REST API
(00:23:04) HTML Frontend for Your API - Jinja2 Templates
(00:59:53) Path Parameters - Validation and Error Handling
(01:36:09) Pydantic Schemas - Request and Response Validation

title: Lec 08: Binary Trees Explained | Data Structures & Algorithm | @systemandcode
description:
Welcome back to the Data Structures & Algorithms series on System And Code! In Lecture 08, we are diving deep into Binary Trees. Building on our knowledge of general trees, we’ll explore why Binary Trees are a cornerstone of computer science and how they differ from other tree structures.

In this video, we cover:

The fundamental definition of a Binary Tree.
Key properties and terminologies (Nodes, Leaves, Depth, and Height).
Detailed breakdown of Binary Tree types: Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced.
Memory representation and how they are structured in code.

Topics Covered: 
Definition of Binary Trees: Understanding the fundamental structure where each node has at most two children (left and right).
Binary Tree Properties: Key characteristics such as the relationship between height and the maximum number of nodes.
Types of Binary Trees:
Full Binary Tree: Every node has either 0 or 2 children.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.
Perfect Binary Tree: All internal nodes have two children and all leaves are at the same level.
Balanced Binary Tree: The height difference between left and right subtrees is minimal.
Degenerate (or skewed) Tree: Each parent node has only one associated child node.
BST: Similarity with Binary search and its overview

title: Reinforcement Learning Components Explained | Agent, Environment, Reward & Policy | VTU Module 5
description:
Welcome to Express VTU 4 All 🎓

In this video, we explain one of the most important Reinforcement Learning questions from Module–05 of Machine Learning (BCS602).

This is a frequently repeated VTU theory question and is considered a high-scoring 8–10 marks question.

📌 Exact Question Covered

Analyze the components of Reinforcement Learning with a neat diagram.

🧠 Topics Covered

✅ Introduction to Reinforcement Learning

✅ Components of Reinforcement Learning

✅ Agent

✅ Environment

✅ State

✅ Action

✅ Reward

✅ Policy

✅ Value Function

✅ Reinforcement Learning Architecture

✅ Exam-Oriented Explanation

📘 Introduction to Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine learning technique in which an agent learns by interacting with an environment and receives rewards or penalties based on its actions.

The objective is to learn an optimal strategy that maximizes cumulative rewards over time.

🌟 Components of Reinforcement Learning
1️⃣ Agent

The Agent is the learner or decision-maker.

Functions:

✔ Observes the environment

✔ Takes actions

✔ Learns from rewards

Example:
Robot
Self-driving car
Chess-playing software
2️⃣ Environment

The Environment is everything outside the agent with which the agent interacts.

Functions:

✔ Provides states

✔ Receives actions

✔ Generates rewards

Example:
Chess board
Road traffic system
Video game world
3️⃣ State (S)

A State represents the current situation of the environment.

Example:

In chess:

Current board configuration.

In self-driving cars:

Current vehicle position and surroundings.

4️⃣ Action (A)

An Action is a decision taken by the agent.

Example:
Move left
Move right
Accelerate
Select a chess move
5️⃣ Reward (R)

A Reward is the feedback received after performing an action.

Example:

+10 → Correct action

-10 → Incorrect action

Purpose:

Guide the agent toward better decisions.

6️⃣ Policy (π)

A Policy defines how an agent chooses actions in different states.

Representation:
π(s)=a

Meaning:

For state s, choose action a.

7️⃣ Value Function

The Value Function estimates the expected future reward from a particular state.

Purpose:

Helps determine how good a state is.

8️⃣ Q-Value Function

The Q-Function estimates the quality of taking a specific action in a given state.

Purpose:

Helps the agent select the best action.

🌟 Neat Reinforcement Learning Diagram
                 Environment
        ┌────────────────────────┐
        │                        │
        │   State (S)            │
        │   Reward (R)           │
        └─────────▲──────────────┘
                  │
                  │
                  │
                  ▼
            ┌─────────┐
            │  Agent  │
            └─────────┘
                  │
                  │ Action (A)
                  ▼
          Environment
🌟 Complete RL Architecture
          Current State
                 │
                 ▼
             Agent
                 │
            Action
                 ▼
          Environment
                 │
       Next State + Reward
                 │
                 ▼
             Agent
🎯 Importance of Components
Component Purpose
Agent Learns and takes decisions
Environment Provides feedback
State Represents current condition
Action Decision taken by agent
Reward Learning signal
Policy Decision-making strategy
Value Function Estimates future reward
Q-Function Evaluates actions

✔ Draw neat RL architecture diagram

✔ Explain each component separately

✔ Give real-world examples

✔ Mention policy and value function clearly

Welcome back to Fun Electronics! ⚡ In this English tutorial, we are diving into the world of Operational Amplifiers (Op-Amps) to build and simulate a Voltage Follower Circuit using Tinkercad.

A voltage follower, also known as a unity-gain buffer, has a voltage gain of 1 (Av = 1). This means the output voltage exactly follows the input voltage. In this video, we'll explain why this circuit is incredibly useful for isolating stages in electronics (thanks to its high input impedance and low output impedance) and show you exactly how to wire it up on a virtual breadboard.

🛠️ What you will learn in this video:

What a Voltage Follower (Unity Gain Buffer) is and how it works.

How to wire an Op-Amp IC on a breadboard in Tinkercad.

How to set up function generators and oscilloscopes to test the circuit.

Proving that Output Voltage = Input Voltage (Vout = Vin).

title: What Are Transistors? How Transistors Work? Discover the Magic Behind Modern Electronics!
description:
Welcome to Club Academia! Where curiosity meets knowledge! In this video, we're diving into the fascinating world of electronic components—the unsung heroes of technology that make our devices come alive. From tiny resistors and capacitors to powerful microchips, we'll explore how these components work together to create the tech we love and rely on every day.

What You'll Learn:
In this video, we’re focusing on one of the most crucial components in electronics: the transistor. Often referred to as the building block of modern electronics, transistors play a vital role in amplifying and switching electronic signals. Here’s a sneak peek at what we’ll cover:

What is a Transistor?

Discover how this semiconductor device functions as a tiny gate that controls the flow of electrical current.
Structure and Functionality:

Learn about the three key terminals of a transistor: Collector, Base, and Emitter—and how they work together to amplify signals.
Types of Transistors:

Understand the two main types: Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs) and Field Effect Transistors (FETs), including their applications and efficiency.
Real-World Applications:

See how transistors are used in various circuits, including audio amplifiers, switching applications for devices like LEDs, and signal modulation in communication devices.

Mind-Blowing Numbers:
Did you know that modern CPUs can contain billions of transistors? For instance, high-end processors may have around 10 billion transistors, while GPUs can reach up to 20 billion or more! The highest recorded count in a consumer microprocessor is a staggering 134 billion transistors in Apple’s ARM-based dual-die M2 Ultra!

7 Fascinating Facts About Transistors:

First Transistor: The first transistor was created in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs.

Miniaturization: Transistors have shrunk dramatically—once the size of a finger, now they can be smaller than a nanometer!

Transistor Count Record: The record for the most transistors on a single chip was set by Nvidia's B100 accelerator, boasting 208 billion MOSFETs as of 2024.

Heat Generation: Transistors generate heat during operation, highlighting the importance of cooling systems in computers.

Quantum Computing: Innovations in transistor technology are paving the way for quantum computing, offering unprecedented processing capabilities.
Analog vs. Digital: Versatile transistors function in both analog and digital applications, playing a crucial role in modern electronics.

Semiconductor Production: In 2021, the semiconductor industry shipped approximately 1 trillion transistors every day!

Why Does This Matter?
Transistors are everywhere! They power everything from smartphones and computers to televisions and household appliances. Understanding how these components work not only enriches your knowledge but also empowers you to appreciate the technology you use daily.

Engage with Us!
If you find this video interesting and informative, please give it a thumbs up! Don’t forget to subscribe to Club Academia for more enlightening content about the world of technology and electronics. If you have any questions or topics you'd like us to cover, drop them in the comments below!

Stay Curious!
At Club Academia, we encourage you to keep questioning and keep learning. Until next time, stay curious!

title: How Transistors Work: The Complete Beginner’s Guide to Amplification & Switching
description:
00:00 Why transistors matter: amplification need, history, and impact
03:10 Active devices and gain: cascading systems, power gain, why passives are not enough
05:30 What a transistor is: three terminals, control terminal, nonlinearity, transresistance idea
07:20 Two control styles: current-controlled (BJT) vs voltage-controlled (FET)
08:50 Two core applications: amplification (small signal to large signal) and switching (two stable states)
14:50 Transistor as an amplifier and as a switch: intuition with I–V curves, stable states, cascading into logic systems

In this video, we build an intuitive and complete understanding of how transistors work as active devices.
This lecture introduces the core ideas behind amplification, switching, and gain — the foundation on which all analog and digital electronics are built.

We start by asking: What makes a device “active”? How does it control current? Why does gain emerge from physical behavior?
Using simple visual reasoning, we connect device physics to circuit-level concepts and show how transistors enable both analog signal processing and digital logic.

Topics covered:
• What makes transistors “active” devices
• How gain arises and why it matters
• Large-signal vs small-signal behavior
• Current control, voltage control, and channel modulation
• How transistors act as switches in digital circuits
• How transistors act as amplifiers in analog circuits
• The link between device physics and higher-level circuit design
• Why amplification is fundamental to all electronics

This lecture is ideal for:
• Undergraduate students learning devices for the first time
• Self-learners and hobbyists exploring electronics
• VLSI and circuit design beginners
• Anyone preparing for university exams or interviews
• Students revising transistor fundamentals before studying MOSFETs

The aim is to give you a clean, intuitive foundation so that concepts like diodes, MOS capacitors, MOSFETs, CMOS logic, and analog design become much easier to understand in later videos.

JavaScript allows developers to add dynamic features like animations, form validation, and interactive content to web pages.

Node.js is a runtime environment that allows you to run JavaScript on the server side (outside of a web browser). Before Node.js, JavaScript was mainly used for client-side scripting, but Node.js enables it to be used for building back-end services like APIs, handling databases, and creating full-stack applications. What is SQL?
SQL stands from Structured Query Language. It is used to communicate with several relational databases such as MySQL, Oracle and MS SQL Server. Using SQL queries, you can fetch, update, delete and manipulate data that is stored in the form of rows and columns. SQL became the de facto standard programming language for relational databases after they emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s. You can also permit users to perform specific tasks on tables, procedures, and views. SQL commands are divided into different types, such as data manipulation language (DML), data definition language (DDL), transaction control language (TCL), and data query language (DQL).

title: Day 16: PostgreSQL 18 Bidirectional Replication Setup #postgresql #ha #bidirectional #rep #day16
description:
🎥 YouTube full video:

https://youtu.be/iWjZwX0cx5M

What is Bidirectional Replication?

Bidirectional Replication (BDR) is a PostgreSQL replication method where two or more databases can simultaneously send and receive data changes, allowing updates on any node to be synchronized with the others.

Use Cases
Active-Active database architecture
High Availability (HA)
Disaster Recovery (DR)
Multi-region/global applications
Branch office synchronization
Load sharing across databases

Benefits

✅ No single point of failure
✅ Reduced downtime
✅ Faster access for global users
✅ Data redundancy and disaster recovery
✅ Read/write operations on multiple nodes
✅ Better scalability and availability

 To set up bidirectional replication between two Master-Slave (Primary-Replica) setups in PostgreSQL 18, we’ll use logical replication with the new features introduced in PostgreSQL 16 and enhanced in 18, such as the origin parameter to prevent infinite loops and improved failover slot synchronization. This example assumes you want bidirectional replication between the two primaries (Primary1 and Primary2), while their respective replicas (Replica1 and Replica2) serve as standby servers for high availability. Below is a step-by-step guide with examples tailored to your architecture.

Architecture Overview

Setup 1: Primary1 (192.168.50.128) ↔ Replica1 (192.168.50.129)
Setup 2: Primary2 (192.168.50.130) ↔ Replica2 (192.168.50.131)

Bidirectional Replication: Primary1 ↔ Primary2 (logical replication)
Master-Slave Replication: Primary1 → Replica1 and Primary2 → Replica2 (physical streaming replication)

We’ll configure:

Physical streaming replication for each Primary-Replica pair (Primary1 → Replica1 and Primary2 → Replica2).
Logical bidirectional replication between Primary1 and Primary2.

Conclusion:

You now have bidirectional logical replication between Primary1 ↔ Primary2 while keeping Primary-Replica setups in place. Let me know if you need refinements!

title: (SQL Tutorial #9) Learn to use ROWNUM in | SQL | Oracle |
description:
You will learn how to use  ROWNUM  in SQL in this video. 
► ROWNUM clause is used to specify the number of records to return.
► Queries used in this video:
1. Display a table
SELECT * FROM hr.employees;
2. Display the first 7 rows only.
SELECT * FROM hr.employees WHERE ROWNUM ▶️7;
3. Display the first 5 rows only and sort by employee_id
SELECT * FROM hr.employees WHERE ROWNUM▶️5 ORDER BY employee_id;
4. Display the first 10 rows only and only the records with department_id = 90 sorted in an ascending order.
5. SELECT * FROM hr.employees WHERE ROWNUM▶️10 AND department_id=90 ORDER BY employee_id ASC;
6. To compare results of OR and AND operators:
SELECT * FROM hr.employees WHERE ROWNUM▶️10 OR department_id=90;
*** ▶️ means less than***

title: Oracle SQL Tutorial - If condition using Decode and Case Statements
description:
In this tutorial, we will see how to use CASE and DECODE to construct an IF ELSE conditions in SQL.

SQL used in this video are given below.  Also, note as mentioned in video, the values we substitute for different data should be of same data type.


select * from emp_test;

Male  Female better than just F

IF gender = 'M' then print 'MALE', gender = 'F' then print 'Female', ELSE, print 'Unknown'

select first_name,gender from emp_test;

select first_name,DECODE(GENDER,'M','Male','F','Female','Unknown') Gender from emp_test;

SELECT first_name,DECODE(GENDER,'M','Male','F','Female') Gender FROM emp_test;

SELECT first_name,
CASE GENDER
WHEN 'M' THEN 'MALE'
WHEN 'F' THEN 'FEMALE'
END AS GENDER
FROM EMP_TEST;


SELECT first_name,
CASE GENDER
WHEN 'M' THEN 'MALE'
WHEN 'F' THEN 'FEMALE'  ELSE 'UNKNOWN'
END AS GENDER
FROM EMP_TEST;



SB - Savings Bank
CA - CURRENT ACCOUNT
FD - Fixed Deposit
LA - Loan ACCOUNT

title: The SQL Query That Replaced 10 Lines of Code
description:
ost analysts write running totals using a self-join. It works — but it's slow, messy, and painful to read.

There's a better way: SUM() OVER (ORDER BY month)

One window function. No join. No subquery. Same result.

Use it for:

Running totals
Moving averages
Percent of total
Save this. Window functions are one of the most underused tools in SQL — and once you learn them, you'll use them everywhere.

The issue thread hit 340 comments. Nobody's changed their mind.

title: Git Tutorial for Beginners - Git & GitHub Fundamentals In Depth
description:
This git tutorial for beginners is designed to teach you the git command line tool and how it works with github. This beginner git tutorial teaches github fundamentals and explains concepts like branches, pushing, merge conflicts and many other useful git commands. It goes through the git workflow and illustrates how git and github work on a lower level.

💻 Git Download: https://git-scm.com/
🖱 GitHub Website: https://github.com/

⌨ Common GitHub Commands ⌨
To create a new repository locally: git init
To add files to staging area: git add .  OR   git add ~filename~
To check status of staging area: git status
To commit new changes: git commit -m "commit message"
To create a new branch: git checkout -b ~branch name~
To switch between branches: git checkout ~branch name~
To merge branches together: git merge ~branch name~
To add a remote repository: git remote add ~remote name~ ~https://yourremoteurl~
To pull changes from a remote repository: git pull ~remote name~ ~branch name~
To push changes to a remote repository: git push ~remote name~ ~branch name~

title: Git Tutorial for Complete Beginners | Learn Git in 35 minutes
description:
Git Tutorial for Complete Beginners | Learn Git in 35 minutes
In this video, we shall cover everything you need to know to start working with Git. Git is a version control system which can be used to track any changes in a repository. 
We shall first understand what is Git and why do we need to use it. We shall then see how to install Git and configure Git. We will also look at the Git Workflow.
In this video, I am going to build a simple digital clock using python. But I will build this project step by step so you can see how I add and commit different changes to git repository. 

Timeline:
00:00 Intro
01:10 What is Git
04:07 How to Install Git
05:52 How to Configure Git
07:39 How to create a Git Repository
10:07 What is Git Branch
11:41 Understanding Git Workflow
12:41 Git add (Adding changes to Git Staging area)
15:10 Git commit (Commit change to Git Repository)
18:29 Git log (Viewing the commit history)
23:16 Creating a Git Branch
26:52 Merge Branch
29:54 How to use Git Reset
31:08 How to use Git Checkout
32:21 Git Detached HEAD state
35:09 Finally comparing changes in multiple git branch 

We shall also see the three layers of git repository i.e. the working directory, staging area and git repository.

I am going explain in detail how to add files to staging area and then remove files form staging area if required. We shall see how to commit changes. We shall also discuss about the significance of git staging area and why we need it.

Finally, we shall see what is a branch and how to create a branch and how to switch between different git branches. I will explain the significance of having multiple branch in your git repository and how we can merge changes from one branch to another.

Merging branch is an important feature of Git so we shall explain git merge by creating a real digital clock project.

This video also covers git reset and git checkout. We use git reset and checkout to point HEAD to a different commit or different version of the repository. We shall see the difference between reset and checkout commands.

Hopefully this video should give you a complete idea about git and how to start working with git.

Welcome to our comprehensive video series on Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS) for ARM microcontrollers! This series is designed for engineers, students, and developers looking to master RTOS concepts, with a focus on ARM Cortex-based microcontrollers. Each video covers crucial topics ranging from architecture design to advanced RTOS features like multi-threading, semaphores, and message queues.

In this series, we’ll dive into the following key topics:

RTOS architecture design: Learn how to structure real-time systems for performance and efficiency.
Input/Output operations: Explore how to manage I/O effectively in RTOS-based systems.
Interrupt handling: Understand how to implement and manage interrupts in real-time applications.
Timers and Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM): Master the use of timers and PWM for precise control.
Serial communication protocols: Work with UART, I2C, and SPI to implement robust communication between devices.
RTX RTOS: Explore the widely-used Keil RTX RTOS for ARM-based microcontrollers and learn how to utilize its core features.
Multi-threading: Learn how to implement and manage multiple threads efficiently in RTOS.
Mutex and semaphores: Ensure thread synchronization and safe resource sharing using mutexes and semaphores.
Message queues and mailbox: Understand inter-process communication with message queues and mailboxes.
Events and flags: Manage event-driven programming using event flags.
Virtual memory management: Learn how to handle virtual memory in RTOS systems for complex applications.
Our in-depth tutorials and practical examples will give you the knowledge you need to design, develop, and optimize real-time systems using ARM microcontrollers.

title: Lecture - VMs & OS
Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) in OS | Deadlock Detection
description:
In this video, we completely explain the Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) in Operating Systems — one of the most visually intuitive and examination-critical tools for Deadlock Detection. We cover the complete notation, how to draw RAGs, how to detect deadlock using cycles in RAGs, the critical difference between Single Instance and Multiple Instance resource cases, the Wait-for Graph, and solved GATE-level examples and previous year questions. If RAG has ever confused you — this is your complete, exam-ready reference lecture.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📌 TOPICS COVERED IN THIS VIDEO
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
✔ Quick Recap — Deadlock & Four Necessary Conditions
✔ What is a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG)?
      → Purpose & Importance of RAG
      → When RAG is used in OS
✔ RAG Components — Complete Notation:
      → Process Nodes — Circles (P₁, P₂, P₃...)
      → Resource Nodes — Rectangles with dots
      → Dots inside Resource = Number of Instances
      → Request Edge — P → R (Process requests Resource)
      → Assignment Edge — R → P (Resource assigned to Process)
✔ How to DRAW a Resource Allocation Graph — Step by Step
✔ DEADLOCK DETECTION USING RAG:

   CASE 1 — SINGLE INSTANCE RESOURCES:
      → Cycle EXISTS → Deadlock CONFIRMED ✅
      → No Cycle → No Deadlock ✅
      → Cycle is NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT condition

   CASE 2 — MULTIPLE INSTANCE RESOURCES:
      → Cycle EXISTS → Deadlock POSSIBLE (NOT guaranteed) ⚠️
      → No Cycle → No Deadlock ✅
      → Cycle is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT condition

title: What is Round Trip Time (RTT) in Computer Networks? | RTT Explained |Networking Basics for Beginners
description:
In this video, we explain Round Trip Time (RTT) – a crucial concept in computer networks and internet communication. If you are a networking student, preparing for IT interviews, or just curious about network performance, understanding RTT is essential.

What is Round Trip Time (RTT)?

Round Trip Time, or RTT, is the total time it takes for a network packet to travel from the source to the destination and back again. It is a key measure of network latency and is used to evaluate the speed and efficiency of data transmission over a network.

Why is RTT Important?

RTT helps determine network performance and reliability.

It indicates the latency between two devices, which is critical for real-time applications like online gaming, video calls, and VoIP.

RTT is used by network protocols such as TCP to adjust timeouts and optimize data transmission.

A higher RTT often indicates network congestion, delays, or inefficient routing.

Factors Affecting RTT

Propagation Delay: Time taken for a signal to travel from sender to receiver.

Transmission Delay: Time required to push all packet bits onto the network.

Processing Delay: Time taken by routers or switches to process packets.

Queuing Delay: Time packets spend waiting in network queues before transmission.

Measuring RTT

A simple way to measure RTT is by using the ping command. For example, typing ping google.com in your command prompt will show the round trip time in milliseconds. This value tells you how quickly your computer can communicate with the target server and receive a response.

RTT in TCP/IP Networks

In TCP/IP networks, RTT is critical because it determines timeout intervals and window size for reliable data transfer. Protocols rely on RTT to manage packet retransmissions and maintain smooth communication.

Real-Life Examples

Online gaming lag occurs due to high RTT between your device and the game server.

Video conferencing delays are often caused by elevated RTT.

Fast-loading websites usually have low RTT, ensuring better user experience.

Conclusion

Round Trip Time is a fundamental concept that affects network speed, reliability, and overall performance. By understanding RTT, network engineers, IT students, and enthusiasts can troubleshoot network issues effectively and optimize data communication.

title: History Lesson: Unforgettable Bhopal Gas Disaster | Documentary | World History #history #summary
description:
A History Lesson: Unforgettable Bhopal Gas Disaster | India | Documentary | World History #history 

#documentary
#summary

Welcome back to our channel, where we dive deep into the folds of history, unravel mysteries, and sometimes, just sometimes, we try to make sense of the world's peculiar events with a dash of humor. Today, we're tackling a topic that, while no laughing matter, will be approached with a tone that keeps you engaged and perhaps slightly amused. Get ready for an animated history lesson on one of the most catastrophic industrial disasters in world history - the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984. So buckle up, as this ride through history won't be your typical classroom lecture.

Let's set the scene: Bhopal, India, 1984. It was a time of big hair, even bigger shoulder pads, and, unfortunately, one of the biggest disasters that the world has ever witnessed. This wasn't your run-of-the-mill disaster documentary subject, nor was it something that could be categorized under natural disasters or abandoned places. Nope, this was a man-made horror story that unfolded in a city caught on camera for the news to broadcast across the globe.

As we weave this scary story, let's not forget the animated history vibe we're going for. Imagine the scene animated with vibrant colors and characters, bringing a unique perspective to the tragedy. This isn't just simple history; it's a complex web of events, decisions, and failures that led to the catastrophic night when the city of Bhopal turned into one of the world's most horrifying abandoned places.

The Bhopal Gas Tragedy wasn't a part of ancient history or something buried in the annals of world history. This disaster documentary tells a tale that feels all too recent, a grim chapter in modern industrialization and a stark reminder of the consequences of negligence and lack of safety measures. It's a story that might make you think, "This is America," but no, this horror unfolded in India, showcasing a global issue of industrial safety and environmental protection.

Through this summary, we aim to educate and entertain, providing facts that paint a vivid picture of the disaster's impact. But let's throw in a conspiracy theory or two, because what's a discussion on a disaster without delving into the mysteries that surround it? Was it merely an accident, or were there darker forces at play? Join us as we explore these theories, not to trivialize the tragedy but to understand the myriad narratives that have spun from it.

Now, onto the scary stories segment - the night of the disaster. Imagine the scene animated, as toxic gas leaks into the unsuspecting city, a real-life horror story worse than any ghost tale. It's a stark reminder of how disasters can strike, turning bustling cities into ghost towns, leaving behind a legacy of pain and loss.

As we wrap up this summary, let's reflect on what this disaster documentary has taught us. The Bhopal Gas Tragedy, while a specific event in history, reflects broader themes of industrial responsibility, environmental ethics, and the human cost of negligence. title: MARCO POLO's Departure | Mini History Documentary  #history #kublaikhan #marcopolo #historyfacts
description:
Welcome to Mini History. A fresh look on Ancient History's most fascinating tales!

He crossed the known world—and changed how Europe understood it forever.

In 1271 AD, a seventeen-year-old Venetian merchant stepped onto a wooden pier and sailed east—toward deserts that sang, cities larger than any Europe had known, and an empire that ruled half the earth.

This is the true story of Marco Polo.

From the markets of Venice to the court of Kublai Khan, Marco Polo spent 24 years crossing deserts, oceans, and empires—serving the Mongol court, witnessing inventions centuries ahead of Europe, and recording a world that many would refuse to believe existed.

Captured in war and imprisoned, he dictated his memories into a book that would reshape maps, ignite imaginations, and inspire explorers for centuries—including Christopher Columbus.

This episode explores:
 • The Silk Road and the Mongol Empire at its height
 • Cities of unimaginable scale and wealth
 • Paper money, coal, porcelain, and global trade networks
 • Why Marco Polo was called a liar—and why history proved him right
 • How one traveler stitched East and West together with words

Discovery is not about arriving somewhere new…
It’s about returning changed.

title: When Britain Fought for the Right to Sell Drugs #history #opiumwar #movie #china #british
description:
When Britain Fought for the Right to Sell Drugs!

In the early 1800s, China stood as the richest nation on Earth, trading silk, porcelain, and tea for silver. But when Britain’s treasure ran dry, greed found a new path. What began as a trade deal turned into one of history’s darkest bargains — a nation flooding another with addiction, all in the name of profit. From royal palaces to opium dens, lives unraveled while empires grew richer. This is the forgotten story of how ambition disguised itself as progress, and how a simple plant reshaped the fate of two great civilizations.

Yet behind the smoke and the silver, a deeper question lingers — what happens when “civilization” itself becomes the weapon? The answer would come in gunfire, treaties, and a war fought not for freedom, but for the right to sell despair. The story ends where the world’s balance begins to shift… and where mercy becomes the most expensive thing of all.

title: The History of Writing - Where the Story Begins - Extra History
description:
📜  The History of Writing - Extra History
Sumer was the land of the first real cities, and those cities required complex administration. The temples that kept people together were not only religious places but also warehouses that stored the community's collective wealth until it was needed to get through lean years. As the donations came in, scribes would count the items and draw pictures of them on clay tablets. The images quickly became abstract as the scribes needed to rush, and they also morphed to represent not just an image but the word itself - more specifically, the sound of the word, which meant that it could also be written to represent other words that sounded similar (homophones). Sumerian language often put words together to express new ideas, and the same concept applied to their writing. As people came to use this system more, the scribes began to write from left to right instead of top to bottom since they were less likely to mess up their clay tablets that way. Those who read the tablets didn't appreciate this change, so the scribes rotated the words 90 degrees allowing tablets to be rotated if the reader preferred - but this made the images even more abstract, until eventually, the pictograms vanished entirely to be replaced by wedge-shaped stylus marks: cuneiform. Many of Sumer's neighbors adopted this invention and helped it spread throughout the region, though completely different writing systems developed independently in cultures situated in places like China and South America!

title: Indian Tax System Explained | Proportional Taxation | Public Finance|UGC NET Economics #shivanshsir
description:
Important topic from Public Finance 📘🔥

Indian Tax System – Proportional Taxation

Proportional Taxation is a system in which the rate of tax remains constant regardless of the income level of the taxpayer.

Under this system, every taxpayer pays the same percentage of income as tax, whether their income is low, medium, or high.

Very important for:
✔️ UGC NET Economics
✔️ Public Finance
✔️ Fiscal Policy
✔️ Taxation System
✔️ Indian Economy
✔️ PYQs & Conceptual MCQs

What is Proportional Taxation? ⚖️

Proportional Taxation (Flat Tax) is a tax system in which all taxpayers pay the same tax rate irrespective of their income level.

✔️ Same tax rate for everyone
✔️ Constant percentage of income paid as tax
✔️ Simple and easy to administer
✔️ Also known as Flat Rate Taxation

Key Features 🔥

✔️ Uniform tax rate for all income groups
✔️ Tax liability increases with income, but tax rate remains constant
✔️ Simple tax structure
✔️ Easy compliance and administration
✔️ Neutral treatment of taxpayers

Examples in India 🇮🇳
Professional Tax

A fixed tax structure applicable to professionals in many states.

Corporate Tax (Flat Rate Structure)

Uniform rate applicable within a category of companies.

Securities Transaction Tax (STT)

Same rate on specified securities transactions.

Equalization Levy

Uniform levy on specified digital services.

How Proportional Taxation Works 📘

Assume the tax rate is 10% for everyone:

Taxpayer A

Income = ₹3,00,000
Tax = ₹30,000

Taxpayer B

Income = ₹10,00,000
Tax = ₹1,00,000

Taxpayer C

Income = ₹50,00,000
Tax = ₹5,00,000

➡️ Tax amount changes with income, but tax rate remains 10% for all.

Advantages ✅

✔️ Simple and easy to understand
✔️ Easy to administer and enforce
✔️ Lower compliance costs
✔️ Reduces tax evasion opportunities
✔️ Encourages investment and economic growth

Disadvantages ❌

✔️ Does not reduce income inequality effectively
✔️ Low-income groups may feel a greater burden
✔️ Ignores the ability-to-pay principle
✔️ Less equitable than progressive taxation
✔️ May not support redistributive objectives

Proportional vs Progressive Taxation ⚖️
Progressive Tax

➡️ Income ↑ → Tax Rate ↑

Proportional Tax

➡️ Income ↑ → Tax Rate Remains Same

Proportional vs Regressive Taxation ⚖️
Proportional Tax

➡️ Same percentage tax for everyone

Regressive Tax

➡️ Effective tax burden falls as income rises

Exam Trick ⚡

Progressive Tax → Rich Pay Higher Rate 📈

Proportional Tax → Everyone Pays Same Rate ⚖️

Regressive Tax → Poor Bear Higher Burden 📉

One Line Revision 📌

Proportional taxation charges the same percentage rate of tax on income irrespective of the taxpayer's income level.

description:
Link to this course:

Introduction to Ancient Philosophy - Ancient Philosophy: Plato & His Predecessors

What is philosophy?  How does it differ from science, religion, and other modes of human discourse?  This course traces the origins of philosophy in the Western tradition in the thinkers of Ancient Greece.  We begin with the Presocratic natural philosophers who were active in Ionia in the 6th century BCE and are also credited with being the first scientists.  Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximines made bold proposals about the ultimate constituents of reality, while Heraclitus insisted that there is an underlying order to the changing world.  Parmenides of Elea formulated a powerful objection to all these proposals, while later Greek theorists (such as Anaxagoras and the atomist Democritus) attempted to answer that objection.  In fifth-century Athens, Socrates insisted on the importance of the fundamental ethical question—“How shall I live?”—and his pupil, Plato, and Plato’s pupil, Aristotle, developed elaborate philosophical systems to explain the nature of reality, knowledge, and human happiness.  After the death of Aristotle, in the Hellenistic period, Epicureans and Stoics developed and transformed that earlier tradition.  We will study the major doctrines of all these thinkers.  Part I will cover Plato and his predecessors.  Part II will cover Aristotle and his successors.

Excellent course, Pr. Sauvé-Meyer keeps the material very engaging, and makes it very clear and easily accessible. Knowing how difficult the original texts are sometimes, this is very valuable.,I was always wanted to know things on Ancient Philosophy, This course has an over all understanding for Plato's work and his students with their different prospective on him and his philosophy.

Introduction: Anaximenes was an important inhabitant of Ionia.
 He is one of the three chief members of the Ionia or the Milesian school. 
He belonged to the era of Pre-Socratic philosophy. 
Very little is known regarding the philosophy of Anaximenes because of his obscure and undocumented work. 
A lot about him and his philosophy is known via the works of other writers on Greek philosophy, specially via the works of Plato and Aristotle. 
Anaximenes and his Arche: For Anaximenes, the air is the fundamental stuff of the universe of which the world is composed of. 
According to him aer (mist, air or vapour) was the primary substance or the arche. 
Arche is a greek word which means, “beginning, first cause, or origin.” 
He chose air to be the fundamental stuff of the universe primarily because of its mobility, changeability, and inner vitality. 
He believed that air is in constant motion due to which it brings development in the course of work of the universe. 
According to Anaximenes, the primarily stuff, air is regulated by the two opposed principles, namely,
Condensation
Rarefaction 
Condensation simply means growing cold. It means compression of the air in a narrow space.
Rarefaction simply means growing hot. In other words, it means the expansion of the air in the greater space. 
It is by rarefaction, air assumes the form of fire and by successive condensation, it gives rise to water, earth and stones.

title: Islamic Philosophy in the Middle Ages - An Introduction
description:
Islamic philosophy is often regarded as a duplication of Greek philosophy. In this video, I explore several terms used by scholars to refer to Islamic philosophy, namely Arabic philosophy, muslim philosophers, philosophy in the Islamic world. In addition, Islamic philosophy is also considered only Islamic theology. I succinctly explain such debatable terms in respect of Islamic philosophy.

Forgive me because the quality of my first video is not good enough. I promise to improve the quality of my next videos gradually.

Henry Corbin, History of Islamic Philosophy, trans. Liadain Sherrard (London & New York: Kegan Paul International)

title: Viktor Frankl's Forbidden Survival Law Why the Strongest Men Are Never Broken | Dark Psychology
description:
The year is 1944. The winter cuts through the Polish mud like a serrated blade. A man stripped of his name, his family, and his identity stands in the freezing gray dawn. He is Viktor Frankl — and he is about to discover the one weapon his captors cannot take. Subscribe — the Warden deploys the armor.

How to stop external chaos from destroying your internal sovereignty.
Why anchoring your survival to external outcomes makes you breakable.
How to transmute suffering into psychological armor no predator can pierce.

Viktor Frankl documented the architecture of psychological collapse inside Auschwitz and emerged with a weapon more dangerous than any physical tool — logotherapy. He proved that the man who finds meaning in his suffering becomes unbreakable, while the man who waits for external salvation is already broken. In 12 minutes, the Warden extracts Frankl's forbidden survival law and deploys
it against the modern predators in your reality.

→ The Architecture of Control: How Auschwitz dismantled identity to extract compliance — and how modern systems use the same blueprint

→ The Nietzsche Axiom: He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how — and how to forge that why in your own arena
→ The Sovereign Space: The microsecond between stimulus and response is the last territory no predator can ever occupy
→ The Alchemy of Agony: How Frankl transmuted torture into data and became psychologically untouchable inside Auschwitz
→ The Modern Audit: Dismantling the corporate machine, the parasitic relationship, and the victim mindset in your present reality

title: The Bill Roll Lecture in Parapsychology featuring Dr  Dean Radin, Fall 2025
description:
Dr. Dean Radin delivers the fall 2025 Bill Roll Lecture entitled "The Next Revolution: Physics, Consciousness, and the Nature of Reality."

Dean Radin is Chief Scientist at the Institute of Noetic Sciences (IONS), Associated Distinguished Professor at the California Institute of Integral Studies, and cofounder and vice chairman of the neuroengineering company, Cognigenics. He earned an MS (electrical engineering) and a PhD (psychology) from the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign. In 2022 he was awarded an Honorary DSc (doctor of science) from the Swami Vivekananda University in Bangalore, India. Before joining the IONS research staff in 2001, Radin worked at AT&T Bell Labs, Princeton University, University of Edinburgh, and SRI International. He has given over 780 talks and interviews worldwide, and he is inventor of 12 patents and author or coauthor  of 340+ scientific and popular articles, book chapters, and books, four of which have been translated into 15 foreign languages: The Conscious Universe (1997), Entangled Minds (2006), Supernormal (2013), Real Magic (2018), and Science of Magic (2025).

"The Next Revolution: Physics, Consciousness, and the Nature of Reality"

Abstract:
Twentieth-century physics overturned the clockwork view of the nineteenth century, and twenty-first-century discoveries are now showing that many of our everyday intuitions about reality are illusions. At fundamental levels, the world looks far stranger than common sense suggests—yet strikingly similar to insights preserved in esoteric traditions. Relativity and quantum mechanics reveal that time and separateness apply only within the narrow band of human-scale experience; outside it, reality behaves in radically different ways. In this talk I will review evidence suggesting that consciousness itself may play an active role in shaping the physical world, and describe how this is being tested. Topics include: (1) experiments using optical interferometers to probe consciousness-related interpretations of quantum theory, (2) results from the long-running Global Consciousness Project, and (3) a growing shift within science toward engaging with metaphysical ideas once considered beyond the pale—including a renewed interest in philosophical idealism.

For more information on previous events, visit the Bill Roll Lecture website: https://www.westga.edu/psychology/bil...

title: Learn English Grammar Fast |A vs An Rules, Exceptions, and Common Mistakes#esl#english#spokenenglish
description:
📚 Confused about when to use "A" and "An" in English grammar? You're not alone! Many English learners make mistakes because they focus on spelling instead of pronunciation.
In this comprehensive English grammar lesson, you'll learn the simple rule that native speakers follow when using indefinite articles. By the end of this video, you'll know exactly when to use A and when to use An, even with tricky words like honest, honor, unique, and urgent.
Whether you're a beginner, student, ESL learner, IELTS candidate, TOEFL candidate, or someone looking to improve spoken and written English, this lesson will help you build a stronger grammar foundation.

What You'll Learn in This Video
✅ What are indefinite articles?
✅ The difference between A and An
✅ Why pronunciation is more important than spelling
✅ How to identify consonant sounds and vowel sounds
✅ Common exceptions to article rules
✅ Real-life examples used in daily English
✅ Common mistakes English learners make
✅ Tips for speaking and writing more naturally

Key Grammar Rules Covered
Use "A" Before a Consonant Sound

Examples:
a story
a place
a bike
a yard
a unique item

Use "An" Before a Vowel Sound

Examples:
an honor
an egg
an artist
an honest person
an urgent call

Important Exceptions Explained
Many learners believe the first letter determines whether to use A or An, but English actually follows pronunciation rules.
Examples:
✔ an honest person
✔ an honor
✔ an hour
Because the "H" is silent.
✔ a university
✔ a unique opportunity
✔ a European country
Because these words begin with a "Y" sound.
Understanding these exceptions can instantly improve your English accuracy and confidence.

Why This Lesson Matters
Correct article usage helps you:
⭐ Speak English more naturally
⭐ Improve grammar accuracy
⭐ Write professional emails
⭐ Score higher in English exams

title: SAT Math Prep: Rational Equation with Cross-Multiplication - Passport to Advanced Math (Algebra)
description:
Here is another SAT Math practice question to prepare for the Passport to Advanced Math section of your SAT exam. 

Solve this rational equation for x:
(x - 2) / (x + 1) = (x + 3) / (x - 4)

Let's use cross-multiplication. The cross-multiplication rule says:

If: a / b = c / d

Then: a * d = b * c

Substitute a, b, c and d. 

So from this:
(x - 2) / (x + 1) = (x + 3) / (x - 4)

We get:
(x - 2) * (x - 4) = (x + 1) * (x + 3)

Calculate this and you get:
x^2 - 6x + 8 = x^2 + 4x + 3

Move the terms to the left side.
x^2 - 6x + 8 - x^2 - 4x - 3 = 0

This simplifies to:
-10x + 5 = 0

Subtract 5 from both sides.
-10x + 5 - 5 = 0 - 5

This simplifies to:
-10x = -5

This means:
x = -5 / -10

x = 1/2

x = 0.5

Let's verify the solution:
(x - 2) / (x + 1) = (x + 3) / (x - 4)

(0.5 - 2) / (0.5 + 1) = (0.5 + 3) / (0.5 - 4)

-1.5 / 1.5 = 3.5 / -3.5

-1 = -1

As previously confirmed, x = 1/2 or 0.5.

title: The absolute value trap that costs students easy points 👀  #testprep #education #math
description:
The absolute value trap that costs students easy points 👀

Drop a 🔥 if you’ve ever rushed an absolute value problem and forgot the negative side.

Here’s the mistake most students make:

They see an absolute value equation and jump straight to one answer.

But absolute value means distance from zero — which means you almost always need to think about two possibilities:

✅ the positive case
✅ the negative case

That’s where students get tripped up.

In this example, going straight to x = 4 or x = -2 isn’t enough. You still have to check which value actually fits the equation and the problem’s context.

Because on the SAT and ACT, the trap usually isn’t the math.

It’s the assumption you make too quickly.

The fix?

Slow down for one second and ask:

“Did I check both sides?”

That one question can save you from losing points on a problem you actually knew how to solve.

Have you ever forgotten the negative solution on an absolute value question? Be honest 👇

title: Same Chord, Different Bass Note, Completely Different Sound! (Chord Inversions) #musictheory #guitar
description:
Every chord can be rearranged. When the root isn't the bass note, that's called an inversion.

In this 22-second lesson, I play C major three ways:

• Root position – C in the bass
• 1st inversion – E (the 3rd) in the bass
• 2nd inversion – G (the 5th) in the bass

Same three notes. Different bass note. Completely different sound.

🎸 This is part 2 of my chord theory series. Start with "What Actually Makes a Chord: Root, 3rd, 5th" and then watch the full "Chords Explained – 5 Theory Rules" lesson on my channel: https://youtu.be/d8y3Nrgwtp4

title: Fix Your Repetitive Melodies Once and For All
channelName: Jason Zac - Nathaniel School of Music
description:
Learn 6 songwriting techniques to break out of a melody trap — stop repeating the same motif and build memorable melodies that grow.

📥 Download our handwritten notes, staff notation and MIDI files and support us on Patreon 🎹🎼✍️https://www.patreon.com/posts/159452533

Ever written a melody that sounds great for two seconds — and then you realise you've been repeating the same motif for the entire verse? You're stuck in a melody trap, and in this lesson Jason walks you through 6 mental techniques to break out of it.

This is a rant-style talking lesson — no keyboards required. Jason explains why your initial melody is just a seed (a motif), and why your job as an artist is to grow it. You'll learn the Mumble Technique — stripping away the lyrics and scatting to expose what the melody is actually doing rhythmically and harmonically.

We break down what makes great melodies timeless using real examples: the octave leap in Somewhere Over the Rainbow, the chord-tone alignment in The Beatles' Hey Jude, the call-and-response structure in nursery rhymes like London Bridge, and the rhythmic genius of modern writers like Taylor Swift and Ed Sheeran. There's also a lovely detour into how Michael Jackson would literally sing the guitar part.

Then Jason shows you how to stress-test your own melody — can you notate it? How many chords does it force you to use? Are you stuck on the root, or can you modulate? Plus the final reality check: play it for non-musicians and see if they latch on to the pulse, the tension, the ebb and flow.

If you're a songwriter, lyric writer, producer, or instrumentalist who keeps falling into the same melodic loops, this lesson will give you the mental tools to escape. Like, share, subscribe, and let us know in the comments which trap you've fallen into most often!

title: 🎼 Grade 1 Music Theory - Treble and Bass Clefs - Lesson 3
description:
Grade 1 Music Theory - Treble and Bass Clefs - Lesson 3

Course notes and worksheet for these lessons here 
Treble and Bass Clefs
https://www.music-online.org.uk/p/lesson-13-treble-and-bass-clefs.html

This lesson will teach you all you need to know about how to use treble and bass clefs for Grade 1 Music Theory at both ABRSM and Trinity College.

Before writing any notes in the treble clef you need to be able to draw the clef neatly for yourself. Bear in mind the following points:

Start around the 2nd line from the bottom and loop around clockwise so that your clef just touches the middle and bottom line. Then slant up to the top looping over just above the top of the stave. Finally bring an almost vertical line down the middle to finish just below the bottom of the stave.

The names of the notes in the spaces of the treble clef can easily be remembered using the word FACE
The 1st space is called F, the 2nd space is called A, the 3rd - C and the 4th - E

The names of the notes on the lines of the treble clef can likewise be remembered using the phrase "Every green bus drives fast"

The drawing of a bass clef is somewhat easier than the treble clef. Nevertheless care must still be taken to make it neat.

The curve is tighter at the top than the bottom. The two dots after the bass clef must be in the top two spaces of the stave.

The names of the notes in the spaces of the bass clef can easily be remembered using the phrase "All Cows Eat Grass"

The names of the notes on the lines of the bass clef can likewise be remembered using the phrase "Grizzly Bears Don't Fear Anything".

title: WTF is a Minor 7 Flat 5 Chord?! 🎸
description:
What in the hell is a Half-Diminished 7 chord? 🎸

Let's learn Bm7♭5.

Half diminished sounds like a chord with low self-esteem 😂

Whoever named this chord did it ZERO favors.

But don't let the name scare you off—this chord is incredibly useful when you want to build tension and create strong resolutions.

Starting with a B minor chord:
• Lower the 5th a half step → B diminished
• Remove the duplicate root
• Lower it a whole step

Boom. Bm7♭5.

Most players know this chord as a Minor 7 Flat 5.

Fun fact:
In the key of C major, Bm7♭5 is the chord standing right outside C major's front door desperately trying to get home.

It's one of the strongest tension-building sounds in music.

And if you think only music theory nerds care about this chord...

The Beatles used it too. 🎸

title: Order of Sharps & Flats #music #musictheory #piano #pianolessons #musiclesson #sharps #flats #order
description:
Order of Sharps & Flats

Each contain 7 letters

Sharps move up in fifths: F-C-G-D-A-E-B

Flats are the same order as the sharps but in reverse! B-E-A-D-G-C-F

It’s helpful to memorize sayings for each. 

One of the more common ones for sharps is:
Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle

For flats: B-E-A-D, Greatest Common Factor

Fingerpicking or fingerstyle guitar is used in virtually all styles of music and therefore is really useful to learn.  Whilst fingerpicking guitar is most associated with acoustic guitar you don't need to learn fingerpicking guitar on an acoustic guitar as it can sound just as good on an electric guitar.  Fingerstyle guitar is used in classical guitar, folk, bluegrass, rock, blues, jazz and virtually any style of guitar you can mention.

This is a series of carefully designed progressive guitar lessons that will carry you through from an absolute beginner on the guitar to a good level of proficiency in fingerstyle guitar.  The GCH Guitar Academy guitar lessons are published to YouTube on a weekly basis just as if you were having private guitar lessons but with the advantage of having the guitar lessons exactly when and where you want them.  This gives you time to practice the lessons on your guitar between lessons so that you get the most from each guitar tutorial and achieve your goals as a guitar player.

You will need some basic knowledge of guitar chords to do this course and basic knowledge of how to read guitar tablature so therefore I recommend you view the following 2 videos before starting on this guitar course.

How to play Wildwood Flower by The Carter Family on guitar.

This is one of the most important songs in American guitar history, made famous by Maybelle Carter and her innovative "Carter Scratch" picking style. While it sounds impressive, the basic melody and picking pattern are much easier to learn than most people think.

In this lesson, I'll break the song into simple sections and show you how the melody fits together so you can start playing this classic country and folk guitar piece with confidence.

A great one to work on if you want to improve your fingerpicking, learn traditional American guitar, and understand one of the foundations of country music.

description:
How to play Time in a Bottle by Jim Croce on guitar.

This is one of those songs that sounds intimidating at first because of one difficult chord shape, but it’s actually much easier than most people think once you understand the movement behind it.

A lot of players get stuck trying to force the chord instead of approaching it the way the song naturally flows. In this lesson, I’ll show you a simpler way to think about the progression that makes the song feel much more playable.

A great one to work on if you want to improve your fingerpicking and learn a classic acoustic guitar song that sounds impressive right away.

title: Personal Finance Basics: The Foundation of Building Wealth
description:
Join me, Albus Wealthmore, as we embark on an enchanting journey to unravel the basics of personal finance together!

In this video, we'll explore the essential topics you need to understand to build and preserve wealth, such as income and expenses, budgeting, saving and investing, credit and debt, insurance, taxes, and planning for retirement.

0:00 Introduction
0:31 Income and Expenses
1:10 Budgeting 101
3:24 Saving vs. Investing
5:29 Credit and Debt
7:06 Insurance
9:19 Taxes
10:46 Retirement

The most basic personal finance skill is tracking your income (money you're making) and expenses (money you're spending). By analyzing your sources of income and expenses, you can create a plan to increase income and/or decrease expenses. Once you have positive cash flow (spending less than you make), you can begin saving and investing. 

Saving is setting aside money without the risk of loss through investment. Since it is low-risk, saving offers low returns on your cash (or zero returns if you're holding money in a checking account). Investing is buying assets with the potential to see high growth but at the risk of losing money through unprofitable investments. 

Credit is your ability to borrow money, which is essential for big purchases like a home. By responsibly utilizing debt, you will increase your creditworthiness, making borrowing money at low interest rates easier. You will find it difficult to borrow money without high credit, and when you do, you'll pay high interest rates.

Obtaining insurance involves paying an insurance provider a monthly premium in exchange for significant financial coverage in emergencies.

My friends, I hope this video helps you increase your financial literacy and happiness!

title: PERSONAL FINANCE GUIDE[ finance basics] [How to achieve financial freedom]
description:
A guide that breaks down the simple personal finance and money concepts. Making the basics of money more understandable. Teaching you How to budget. How to make passive income . How to invest
Financial literacy is not a hard concept to grasp and it is likely that you do know what to do to properly manage your finances. however you might not know how to go about it, or you might not understand what the terms might mean. In this video I will explain the basics of personal finance and some commonly used terms. Hey everyone and welcome to OL better life where we discuss everything personal finance and personal development, in this video we will discuss the difference between saving and investing as well as the benefits of both, budgeting and passive income
Passive and Active income 
There are two different types of income or income you can earn. passive income and  active income.  active income is the most popular way to earn income however it is not the easiest way to earn money. With active income you trade your time for money. You might work a 9-5 to receive a salary at the end of the month or a wage at the end of the week or you mikghtg be a freelancer. People who want to achieve financial freedom quicker or just in general usually don’t make their million and billions from active income because hours in a day are limited. They usually make passive income which is income that requires little to no effort to earn or maintain. Passive income could be dividends or rental income or rentals. I would say earning income is the step that most people stop at when it comes to finances they just spend it and waste their money
Budgeting.
When you earn your money , its important to manage it well. Check what your expenses are and whether your income can support it. You should always live within or below your means never above your means.  this means if you earn 1000 dollars a month you should spend 1000 dollars or less and not 1200 dollars. Budgetting is not just planning on what youll spend your money on but also tracking your spending and using your budget as guidance. Whenever you have to make a big spending decision your budget will prevent you from making impulse buys that you will regret later. Most people budgets have one source of income and then a thousand expenses with not mch money saved or put aside for investing. It is important to try find a way to have more then one source of income, I plan to do a video in the future explaining ways to have muiltiple income streams so subscribe for that.
Saving. Short term 
Budgeting will assist  you with saving. Most people do not save because they do not see the purpose or lack the discipline to do so, I remember I would save money and then as soon as an expense came up that wasn’t eve that important I would spend it, I was treating my savings as left over money which is the wrong mindset. Its important to save for rainy days as you don’t want to take unnecessary loans, you could save for big purchases or you could save for future investment.  There is the notion that saving is useless and investing is the best thing you could do which is not true because any investment is risky and sometimes you might be in a rush to make an investment to avoid having cash that you might make bad investments. Saving is usually for the short term if you are saving up for something specific or it can be long term such as for retirement or emergencies you never know could happen 
Investing long term
As much as saving is great, Saving is not enough no one ever got rich from saving because inflation exists unless your savings are earning an interest. Nonetheless most investments have a higher return then then saving. The stock markets have a &% return, real estate fluctuates but one thing that’s for sure is investment is a good investment. Investing also gives you the opportunity to make passive income and I recently did a video on how to make passive income so go watch it if you haven’t. Investing is usually long term and it will not be a make you rich overnight
 That is my basic guide to finance of course I did not go in depth in this video however I feel like personal finance tends to get a bit overwhelming so this is a great beginner video and its lowkey common sense, you can search for videos on each of these points to learn about them more in depth 
Thank you for watching if this made your life better please make sure to like comment and subscribe for more personal finance and development videos
